adversarial_test_results.prompt:
For most of the nineteenth century the valley was known only to the shepherds who moved their flocks up the slope each spring and down again before the first snow. Travellers who crossed the pass wrote about the silence, the thin air and the strange blue light that settled on the ridge at dusk. A road was surveyed in the eighteen-fifties, but the engineers abandoned the work after two winters of landslides and the maps kept the dotted line of the intended route for another generation. When the railway finally arrived it came from the other side of the mountains, following the river through a gorge that the shepherds had never bothered to name. The station buildings were built of local stone and roofed with slate, and for a while the village below the pass had a hotel, a bakery and a school with a single classroom.
The decades that followed were not kind. Freight moved to the roads, the branch line lost its passenger service, and the timetable shrank to a single goods train a week before that too disappeared. The school closed in the winter of a year nobody now agrees on, and the children were driven down the valley to a larger town where the classes were crowded and the teachers changed every term. Some families left altogether; others stayed and took work in the quarries, which paid badly but kept the houses warm. The hotel became a store, then a storehouse, then nothing that anyone recorded, and the platform lamps were taken away one by one until only the brackets were left. Today the station is a private house with a platform still visible under the grass, and the line of the old railway can be followed on foot for most of its length if you know where to look. Walkers often ask the farmer at the bottom of the valley whether the track goes all the way over the pass, and he tells them that it does, though he has never walked it himself and cannot say what condition it is in beyond the second bridge. The path is steep in places and the markings are poor, and anyone who sets out late in the day is advised to turn back before the light fails, because there is no shelter on the upper slopes and the mist comes down quickly once the sun has gone.

In winter the wind pressed against the glass hard enough to make the whole tower hum, and the keeper learned to sleep through it. Visitors were rare and were treated as an event, with the good cups brought out and the lamp lit early so that the boat could find the channel on the way back. When the service automated the light, the last keeper stayed on for a year to keep the records straight and then left with a box of ledgers, a barometer and no regrets that anyone could detect.
